extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and scholars of contemporary Chinese literature; creative writers interested in Yan Lianke's methods
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the creative-writing principles and stylistic/theoretical criteria associated with Yan Lianke as described on his Wikipedia page, including his coinage 'mythorealism', approaches to plot causality, satire, research for fiction, and use of setting and character. Useful for writers/students studying or emulating his techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mythorealism (general characteristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mythorealism is a Yan coinage described as a blending of stylistic, formal, and narrative elements to create a singular literary reality that diverges from traditional realist representations; Yan describes it as a 'creative process' whose aim is to 'surpass realism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mythorealism 'abandons the seemingly logical relations of real life and explores a "nonexistent" truth, an invisible truth, and a truth concealed by truth.' It 'keeps a distance from any prevailing realism' and relies on 'authors' extraordinary fabrications based on reality.' Methods/channels include imaginations, metaphors, myths, legends, dreams, fantasy, demonization, and transplantation born from everyday life and social reality. (Quotes and paraphrase from the Wikipedia article's summary of Yan's definition.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejecting traditional narrative practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Abandon linearity, straightforward logical cause-and-effect relationships, and strict verisimilitude in favour of nontraditional narrative structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page states mythorealism 'involves rejecting traditional narrative practices, for example linearity, logical cause-and-effect relationships, and, to a certain degree, verisimilitude itself.' Use non-linear plots and structures to explore 'invisible' or 'nonexistent' truths rather than literal realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiation of causal relations in plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify and employ different kinds of causal relations in fiction: 'full causal relations', 'zero causal relations', 'half causal relations' and 'inner causal relations'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Yan's book Discovering Fiction 'advocates the differentiation of "full causal relations", "zero causal relations", "half causal relations" and "inner causal relations" in the plots of fiction' and designates this discovery part of his mytho-realism. Use this toolkit to construct plots that do not rely solely on transparent external cause-and-effect but may emphasize inner, ambiguous, absent, or partial causality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representing 'invisible reality' / 'realism of the spirit(s)'
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to represent 'the invisible reality', 'the reality that is covered up by reality', and 'the non-existing reality'—a 'Realism of the spirit(s)' that transcends surface realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Yan advocated a 'Realism of the spirit(s)', purporting that literature should represent deeper or hidden realities. In practice this leads to plots and imagery that foreground suppressed or spiritual truths rather than only material or documentary facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of imagination and mythic/spiritual elements as methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Infuse fiction with imaginations, metaphors, myths, legends, dreams, fantasy, demonization, and transplantation drawn from everyday life and social reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists these techniques explicitly as 'mythorealist methods and channels.' Writers should deliberately blend quotidian details with mythic or dreamlike elements to produce the 'mythorealist' effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire as social and political critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ satire to critique political and social conditions (e.g., Mao-era China), using provocative, absurd, or carnivalesque depictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Yan's work is 'highly satirical' and has resulted in bans and controversy; the page notes his satire of Mao-era China and ideological positions and that such satire 'provoked surprise in his readers and critics' and led to censorship. Expect tension with authorities and possible controversy when using this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immersive research/fieldwork to ensure accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform close research and immersion (ethnographic-style fieldwork) to capture realistic details even in imaginative works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for Dream of Ding Village Yan 'visited people with AIDS and even lived with villagers for periods of time to make sure the novel was accurate.' Guidance: combine imaginative techniques with grounded research when portraying social realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurring/central fictional setting as literary anchor
rubrics_metrics.description: Create and repeatedly use a distinctive fictional landscape or setting (e.g., Balou Mountain) that becomes the central terrain of the author's literary world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page highlights Balou Mountain as 'the most important setting of Yan's literary world' and notes its use across multiple works (the 'Balou Mountain Series'). Such a recurring setting can provide cohesion, a recognizable imaginative geography, and a platform for varied mythorealist experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breaking norms and innovating structure and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Be willing to break literary norms, vary styles, and create new structures and linguistic forms across works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page says Yan's novels 'have displayed a new structure and linguistic style' and that his 'readiness to break norms' differentiates him from other writers. This approach can lead to a diverse body of work but also to debate, controversy, and mixed critical reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend Western and Chinese elements while remaining grounded in tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate both Chinese and Western literary elements but root the work primarily in Chinese cultural and literary tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: University of Alberta scholar Haiyan Xie is quoted: 'mythorealism incorporates both Chinese and Western literary elements while remaining primarily grounded in Chinese cultural and literary tradition.' Guidance: use cross-cultural influences thoughtfully so the work retains a clear cultural grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray psychologically complex, surprising protagonists
rubrics_metrics.description: Create protagonists who are strange in behavior and psychologically twisted or complex, provoking surprise and debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes Yan's protagonists are 'strange in behavior, and psychologically twisted and complex,' contributing to the grotesque, absurd, and carnivalesque tone. Such characterization may challenge readers' expectations and norms of sympathetic identification.
